extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (ethics, metaphysics)
extracted.subtask_description: An extended philosophical exposition (excerpt) on the nature of the will, character, repentance, deliberation, and suffering—explaining how knowledge, motives, and character determine action and moral self-understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repentance is corrected knowledge, not change of will
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance never proceeds from a change of the will (which is impossible), but from a change of knowledge; the discovery through fuller knowledge that an action did not conform to one's will is repentance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repentance extends to worldly means and ethical judgments; it proclaims itself by making amends for the past as far as possible. Example/analogy: acting egoistically under the false conviction of future reward is corrected when one acquires fuller knowledge (a 'good bill of exchange at a very long date' analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anguish of conscience vs repentance
rubrics_metrics.description: Anguish of conscience is pain at the knowledge of oneself in one’s inmost nature (as will); it is not repentance and will not cease if the will itself remains unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the will were changed (i.e., genuine repentance), the anguish would cease because the past could no longer give pain; thus anguish indicates continued identity of will rather than corrective knowledge alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge is the medium of motives and determines action
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge, as the medium of motives, exerts decisive influence on the appearance of the will in actions; ignorance of circumstances robs them of influence, while imaginary circumstances can act as if real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because motives are mediated through knowledge, differences in what an actor knows can explain different actions despite an unaltered will. This underpins how character shows different features over time as knowledge grows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human deliberation = battle of abstract motives (not libertarian free will)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human 'choice' or deliberation is the thoroughly-fought-out battle between several motives (abstract ideas), the strongest of which then determines the will with necessity; this is not freedom from causal determination in particular volitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberation requires motives to assume the form of abstract thoughts so they can be weighed 'in abstracto'; apparent freedom of particular volitions is the visible result of this internal conflict, not an independence from causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between brute and human motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Brutes are determined by perceptible motives (present impressions) while humans, through reason, are determined by abstract ideas allowing deliberation and foresight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because brute motives and effects are directly perceptible, necessity appears plain in animals; human motives are often abstract and hidden even to the actor, producing the experience of choice and more complex suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (intelligible/empirical) unalterable and determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: The empirical character is the temporal unfolding of an intelligible (extra-temporal) will and is essentially unalterable; it necessarily determines the ethical content of conduct and the manner in which one responds to motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should not infer from this determinism that improvement is useless; instead, the resolve that follows conflict reveals what kind of person one is. The claim is that essential tendencies persist and shape actions across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired character = self-knowledge and deliberate alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'acquired character' is the most perfect practical knowledge of one's individuality—distinct knowledge of one's unalterable qualities, strengths, and weaknesses—and allows one to conduct life deliberately in accordance with one's nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To acquire character one must learn by experience what one desires and can do; thereafter one applies general principles to particular cases, avoids unsuitable pursuits, fills gaps produced by caprice, and thus attains steadiness and success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deeds, not wishes, reveal character
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the deed (as a considered human action) is a valid indication of character for oneself and others; wishes are immediate, present impressions and indicate what man in general is capable of, not the individual's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because deeds typically require deliberation and abstract motives, they reflect intelligible maxims of conduct; unconsidered actions occupy an intermediate position between mere wish and deliberate resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: True repentance must manifest in reparative action
rubrics_metrics.description: True repentance shows itself as action and making amends for the past 'as far as is possible'; mere feeling or anguish is insufficient to constitute genuine repentance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repentance is described functionally: the cognitive correction (knowing the relation of act to intention) motivates reparative deeds; without outward corrective action, repentance is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deception and prearranged 'errors'
rubrics_metrics.description: To deceive oneself, people often prearrange what seem like hasty errors but are in fact secretly considered actions; we deceive and flatter ourselves more cleverly than we deceive others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert that some impulsive-seeming acts are rationalizations; apparent mistakes may be consciously planned to preserve self-image or avoid responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renunciation and focused pursuit as requirement for success
rubrics_metrics.description: To pursue any definite aim (pleasure, honour, wealth, science, art, virtue) seriously and successfully one must renounce innumerable other claims; one cannot make life's path an extended surface by snatching at everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel: identify what suits your individuality, renounce incompatible pursuits, and devote yourself to the chosen line; otherwise one becomes capricious ('will o' the wisp') and attains nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know what you will and what you can do
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere will and ability are insufficient; one must also know what one wills and knows what one can do—only then will one show character and accomplish something rightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This involves honest appraisal of capacities and limits; without it one is 'without character' and liable to repeated failures and subsequent repentance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation and dissimulation are morally perverse
rubrics_metrics.description: It is perverse to try, by reflection, to become something other than one is; the imitation of others' qualities is shameful and a judgment of one's own worthlessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical ethical injunction: avoid playing with 'base coin' (false display of powers); authenticity and alignment with one's nature are morally and practically superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human suffering arises chiefly from abstract thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The causes of human pain and pleasure largely lie not in the real present but in abstract thoughts; mental suffering (anticipation, reflection) is often far greater than physical pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: people may inflict physical pain on themselves to distract from mental anguish; suicide can be easy in despair because mental suffering renders physical pain insensible. This explains why deliberative beings suffer more than brutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will's striving is endless; no final satisfaction exists
rubrics_metrics.description: The will always strives; striving is its sole nature, and it is not susceptible of any final satisfaction—there is no final end of striving and thus no measure or end of suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metaphysical claim grounds ethical options: at the summit of self-knowledge the will can either persist in its previous aims (with knowledge as motive) or make knowledge into a 'quieter' that suppresses willing (self-renunciation).
